quote: $\int_0^\alpha f(x) \sin_{\cos} nx\, dx$ in eine semiconvergente Reihe nach Potenzen von $\frac{1}{n}$
english: [Expand] the integral from 0 to alpha of f(x) sin (or cos) nx dx into a semiconvergent series in powers of 1/n.
topic: The page notes the task of expanding a Fourier-type integral into a semiconvergent series in powers of 1/n, gives a simple continuous nowhere-differentiable function defined via quaternary and binary expansions, lists references on continuous maps of a line onto a surface (space-filling curves), and proposes classifying plane curves of order n by their numbers of even and odd real branches.

triage.modern_statement: Find the asymptotic expansion of the finite Fourier integrals I_s(n)=∫_0^α f(x) sin(nx) dx and I_c(n)=∫_0^α f(x) cos(nx) dx as n→∞, in inverse powers of n. In modern terms: for smooth f on [0,α], repeated integration by parts gives ∫_0^α f(x)e^{inx}dx ~ Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k [f^{(k)}(α)e^{inα} − f^{(k)}(0)]/(in)^{k+1}. Only the endpoints contribute. The series is generally divergent but asymptotic ('semiconvergent' in 19th-century terms, in the Poincaré/Stieltjes sense). Taking real and imaginary parts gives the sin and cos cases.
triage.answered_by: This is a standard classical result, not a discovery credited to one person. The general theory of asymptotic ('semiconvergent') series was set out by Poincaré and Stieltjes in 1886. For smooth f, the expansion of a Fourier integral in powers of 1/n follows from repeated integration by parts. Erdélyi's monograph 'Asymptotic Expansions' (1956) and his work on Fourier integrals treat it systematically, including singular cases (endpoint singularities, logarithmic singularities, van der Corput-type critical points). It now appears in standard textbooks and lecture notes on asymptotic methods.

evidence.claim: Modern asymptotic-methods lecture notes treat the asymptotics of Fourier-type integrals by integration by parts, which gives an expansion in inverse powers of the large parameter from the endpoint contributions.
There is a textbook chapter titled 'Integration by Parts and Asymptotics of Some Fourier Transforms', showing the technique is standard.
Erdélyi's 'Asymptotic Expansions' (1956) presents methods for the asymptotic evaluation of integrals that contain a large parameter.
Erdélyi also wrote 'Asymptotic Expansions of Fourier Integrals Involving Logarithmic Singularities', which extends the theory beyond smooth integrands.
The term 'semiconvergent' for divergent asymptotic series is attributed to Stieltjes (1886), the same year as Poincaré's Acta Mathematica paper on asymptotic series.
A historical thesis covers divergent series and asymptotic expansions from 1850 to 1900, including Poincaré's 1886 paper, which places Hilbert's note in that period.

triage.why: The note asks for a routine asymptotic expansion of a finite Fourier integral in powers of 1/n. For smooth f, integration by parts settles it completely: the coefficients come from the derivatives of f at the endpoints 0 and α. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The term 'semiconvergent' fits the Stieltjes/Poincaré theory of 1886. Later work by Erdélyi and others made this textbook material and covered non-smooth integrands. Research on uniform and singular asymptotics of oscillatory integrals continues, but this particular question is not open. I did not find any source that refers to Hilbert's note itself, and I can't say why it was left open on the page.
